title: Crop Circles: Why Did Two Old British Men Confess in 1991 That They Made Them?
description:
In the late 1970s, on a Friday evening in southern England, two landscape painters finished their last drink and walked into a wheat field carrying an iron bar (by an insider's account), where they pressed out a circle about 9 meters across. For three whole years after that, nobody noticed.

This episode goes through the file in the order things happened and came to light: the iron bar replaced by a wooden plank and a wire loop on a baseball cap; the first newspaper story, around 1980; a meteorologist's plasma vortex hypothesis and the book that sold more than 50,000 copies; the circles the two kept adding, hoping to prove they had nothing to do with weather, and the straight lines that appeared later; the circle in Kent in September 1991 that was judged "impossible for humans to make"; the second wave of creators and the commercial commissions after the confession; the two sides of the 45-minute story beside Stonehenge; and finally the farmers' losses, the tourist trade, and criminal damage in law.

Every circulating version is labeled with who said it and in what year; where sources contradict each other, we say so, and where there is no settled answer, we say that too. Making a crop circle damages someone else's crop; the methods in this video are a record, not an invitation. The source of every number, year and quotation is listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. The two men and the other modern-day people in the video are drawn with no face and no name, appearing only from behind, as hands, or as distant figures.

Information as of 2026-10-10

cl1a.text: The late 1970s, southern England, on a Friday evening.

cl1c.text: Landscape painters Doug and Dave finish a last drink.

cl1e.text: By an insider's account, Doug carries an iron bar into the field.

cl1g.text: They press a circle about 9 meters wide, as if a UFO had landed.

cl1k.text: For the first 3 years, no one noticed.

cl1m.text: But what came next was stranger.

cl1n.text: Over a decade on, in Kent, a researcher stares at the pair's circle.

cl1o.text: Later, legend says, a doctor in a small plane

cl1o2.text: within about 45 minutes, flew twice over a field by Stonehenge.

cl1p.text: And Doug, who walked in that night, said in old age he regretted one thing.

cl1l.text: So why, in 1991, did they speak up themselves?

cl2a.text: They didn't stop. Year after year, back to the fields.

cl2j.text: Doug's iron bar was swapped for a wooden plank, over a meter long.

cl2k.text: Doug holds a string at the center.

cl2m.text: One lap, and the crop falls.

cl2n.text: A baseball cap's peak had a wire loop, for sighting.

cl2o.text: That's all the gear: one night, two men.

cl2p.text: The field wasn't theirs. The crop they ruined was someone else's.

cl2q.text: We'll settle that bill at the end.

cl2r.text: His wife was the first to notice,

cl2r2.text: by Doug's own account, the car's mileage gave him away.

cl2s.text: He got out his scrapbook and took her to a field.

cl2t.text: Only then did she believe the circles were his.

cl2u.text: Around 1980, a newspaper finally wrote about it.

cl2v.text: An obituary later cited its headline.

cl3a.text: Once it ran, some began to study the circles seriously.

cl3a2.text: UFO fans said they were landing marks, just as the pair first intended.

cl3b.text: A meteorologist offered a weather explanation.

cl3c.text: An atmospheric effect, he argued: spinning air flattening the crop.

cl3d.text: Carrying charged matter, it pressed down on the wheat.

cl3e.text: He named his hypothesis the plasma vortex.

cl3f.text: A retired engineer took a different path.

cl3g.text: He and a partner wrote a book on the circles.

cl3j.text: The two hoped to prove weather had no part in it.

cl3k.text: They turned one circle into a set of several.

cl3l.text: Later, straight lines appeared in the designs.

cl3m.text: The meteorologist conceded line designs were man-made.

cl3n.text: Yet simple rings, he said, could still be atmospheric.

cl3o.text: In 1991, a physicist also had something to say.

cl3p.text: Crop circles are either hoaxes or air vortices.

cl3r.text: How many did they make? Britannica says over 200.

cl3s.text: A physics magazine says they admitted to 250.

cl3t.text: TIME says as many as 25 to 30 new ones each season.

cl3u.text: Enthusiasts even sought state research funding.

cl3v.text: Remember this; it comes back later.

cl4a.text: That September, the two decided to come clean.

cl4e.text: That year, Doug was 67 and Dave was 62.

cl4f.text: A reporter took them to Kent.

cl4g.text: With the reporter watching, the two made a circle.

cl4h2.text: Who would he bring to see it?

cl4i.text: It was the researcher who wrote that book.

cl4j.text: He gazed at the flattened crop.

cl4k.text: In the field, the researcher from the intro said no human could do this.

cl4l.text: The two who made it stood right behind him.

cl4m.text: Doug said, I'm afraid we've been having you on.

cl4n.text: The researcher said, we have all been conned.

cl4d.text: September 9: the story hit a British tabloid.

cl4q.text: The headline: Men Who Conned the World.

cl4r.text: Later, in a Hampshire field, they redid it for the press.

cl4s.text: Another researcher said: nothing to impress us,

cl4v.text: He said they'd made some, but the phenomenon remained.

cl4w.text: He even shot back: Canada has crop circles too.

cl4x.text: So were they really the only circle makers?

cl5b.text: They weren't the only ones; others were already in the fields.

cl5c.text: That summer, others made designs the two couldn't.

cl5d.text: A later circle maker said he made his first circle that very summer.

cl5e.text: Their designs inspired a second wave of creators.

cl5f.text: The next year, the two old men won an Ig Nobel Prize.

cl5g.text: The citation: the geometrical destruction of English crops.

cl5h.text: But the fields were no longer about them.

cl5i.text: But that's not the strangest part.

cl5j.text: In July 1996, a formation appeared next to Stonehenge.

cl5l.text: In the popular version, at 5:30 p.m. the field was still empty.

cl5n.text: The doctor from the intro passed again 45 minutes later, and there it was.

cl5o.text: So some said: that fast, it can't have been people.

cl5q.text: In an interview, a circle maker gave another version.

cl5r.text: It was made the night before, by three people, in about 2 hours 45 minutes.

cl5s.text: He said the doctor just missed it on the first pass.

cl5t.text: He didn't say he made it.

cl5p.text: Both accounts come from the same interview.

cl5u.text: The interview wasn't recorded either; both are one-sided.

cl5v.text: That same month, another formation had 194 circles.

cl6a.text: Designs got harder, and then people began paying.

cl6b.text: An art group openly took jobs making crop circles for ads.

cl6c.text: Clients included a cereal brand, a phone company and a TV show.

cl6d.text: A maker said one newspaper job paid the farmer £6,000.

cl6e.text: The flattened crop was worth about a sixtieth of that.

cl6f.text: In 1998, a TV crew filmed them making circles.

cl6g.text: A team pressed a design of 100 circles.

cl6i.text: Complex designs had up to 2,000 separate shapes.

cl6j.text: Even then, some still looked for another cause.

cl6k.text: One researcher said stalk nodes inside circles were elongated.

cl6l.text: He guessed electromagnetic radiation heated them.

cl6m.text: Critics said his statistics and sampling were flawed.

cl6n.text: They said flattened wheat grows differently anyway.

cl6o.text: A physicist was the most honest:

cl6p.text: The studies were neither confirmed nor disproved.

cl6q.text: Over all those years, nobody ever counted one thing.

cl7o.text: That uncounted thing first went to court in 2000.

cl7o2.text: A circle maker pleaded guilty and was fined £100.

cl7n.text: Wiltshire Police say it is criminal damage.

cl7q.text: The plank's story is a record, not an invitation.

cl7j.text: A circle in a field brings the village more visitors.

cl7k.text: In 2004, a visitor center worker said:

cl7l.text: 85 to 90 percent of summer business is tied to crop circles.

cl7a.text: Remember the bill we saved for the end?

cl7c.text: In 2017, a circle about 60 meters wide flattened two acres of wheat.

cl7e.text: The farmer put out a bucket for visitors to donate.

cl7g.text: The Guardian's count: from 2018 to 2022, 92 circles.

cl7i.text: The flattened farmland: over 40 football pitches.

cl7r.text: What became of the two old men?

cl7t.text: That late-life regret from the intro was telling everyone.

cl7u.text: An insider imagined him saying: it's only flattened crop.

cl7v.text: To me, the most interesting part isn't who did it.

cl7w.text: It's why, after the reveal, people still don't believe.

cl7za.text: This file can be archived, but not every circle is claimed.

cl7y.text: Why they talked? TIME says because of that funding.

cl7z.text: An obituary says going public was Dave's idea.

cl7zb.text: Years on, the record leaves it open.

cl7zc.text: As a kid, who did you suspect? Tell me.

cl7zd.text: This channel sticks to the record. Subscribe to open files with us.
